Confession of Sin
kun-FESH-un uv sin
noun phrase (acknowledgment of sin to God)
From the Latin confessio, an acknowledgment, from confiteri (to acknowledge fully); the believer's humble acknowledgment of sin before God, with a view to pardon and cleansing.

Biblical Definition

Confession of sin is the believer's honest and humble acknowledgment of his sin before God, owning it as sin, taking God's side against himself, and seeking pardon and cleansing through Christ. It is grounded in the gospel promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” The wisdom of Proverbs sets confession against concealment: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.” David traces the whole experience in the Psalms—the misery of unconfessed sin, when his bones waxed old through his roaring all the day long, and the relief of acknowledgment: “I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid… and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” True confession is more than admitting facts; it is the broken and contrite heart that names sin honestly, hates it, and forsakes it. The dictionary distinguishes the biblical doctrine from the Roman sacrament of auricular confession, in which sins are confessed to a priest for absolution and assigned penance; Scripture directs confession to God through the one Mediator, with mutual confession among believers commended for healing and prayer, but never a priestly tribunal as the appointed channel of forgiveness. Nor is confession a mere therapeutic unburdening that eases the conscience without repentance. It is the godward acknowledgment of sin by a soul that trusts the faithful and just God to forgive for Christ's sake, the daily exercise of the justified sinner who still walks in a body of death.

Webster 1828 Definition

The believer's humble, godward acknowledgment of sin, owning it and forsaking it, seeking pardon and cleansing through Christ (1 John 1:9); distinct from Roman auricular confession and from mere therapeutic unburdening.

CONFESSION OF SIN, noun phrase. [Latin confessio, acknowledgment.] The humble owning of sin before God for pardon and cleansing.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us” (1 John 1:9).

He that covereth his sins shall not prosper; whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy (Proverbs 28:13).

It is the broken and contrite heart that names, hates, and forsakes sin.

Directed to God through Christ, not to a priest for sacramental absolution.

Key Scripture

1 Jo 1:9 — "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

Pr 28:13 — "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy."

Ps 32:5 — "I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the LORD; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah."

Ps 51:3 — "For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me."

Modern Corruption

Rome channels confession through a priest's tribunal and penance, while the therapeutic age reduces it to an unburdening that eases the conscience without repentance or forsaking of sin.

expand to see more

The Roman sacrament of penance requires the confession of mortal sins to a priest, who pronounces absolution and assigns satisfaction, making the priesthood the appointed channel of forgiveness. The dictionary rejects this on the ground of the one Mediator: there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the believer confesses his sin directly to God through Him. Scripture commends believers confessing their faults one to another for prayer and healing, but it knows no priestly tribunal whose absolution forgives sins; that prerogative belongs to God alone.

The fashionable corruption is therapeutic. Confession is recast as catharsis—an unburdening that relieves guilt feelings, validates the self, and asks no repentance. But biblical confession takes God's side against the sin, hates it, and forsakes it; the one who only covers his sin or merely vents it shall not prosper. The dictionary recovers confession as the godward acknowledgment of a broken and contrite heart that trusts the faithful and just God to forgive for Christ's sake—not a technique for feeling better, but the honest repentance of a soul that has seen its sin as God sees it.

Hebrew Roots

From the Latin confiteri (to acknowledge fully) and the Greek homologeo (to say the same thing, to agree); to confess sin is to say the same of it that God says.

expand to see more

Homologeo, Greek, to confess, literally “to say the same thing,” to agree with God about sin.

Confiteri, Latin, to acknowledge or own fully, the root of “confession.”

Yadah, Hebrew, to confess or acknowledge, used in the penitential Psalms.

Nashbar / dakka, the “broken and contrite” heart of Psalm 51:17.

“Faithful and just” (1 John 1:9) grounds forgiveness in God's character and Christ's satisfaction.

Usage

"The pastor led the congregation in confession of sin, that they might take God's side against themselves."

"He distinguished biblical confession to God from the Roman tribunal of the priest."

"She found that covering her sin brought misery, but confessing and forsaking it brought mercy."
